name: Sulforaphane
summary: Sulforaphane is a sulfur-containing compound formed from glucoraphanin, a precursor found in broccoli and other cruciferous vegetables. Supplements may supply sulforaphane itself or ingredients intended to produce it. A glucoraphanin label is not a measurement of sulforaphane delivered to the body.
commonUses: May activate the Nrf2 antioxidant pathway
May help the body clear air pollutants
roles: The enzyme myrosinase converts glucoraphanin into sulforaphane.
Plant enzymes and gut microbes can contribute to this conversion, so the preparation affects exposure.

status.note: This basic guide does not provide a routine status test.

high.note: See the cautions below; this guide does not establish a safe upper amount.

foodSources.note: Preparation matters: chopping and waiting, or adding raw mustard seed (a source of myrosinase), changes how much is formed.

forms.name: Sulforaphane
forms.note: Supplies the compound itself; its stability and the finished formulation matter.

forms.name: Glucoraphanin
forms.note: Supplies the precursor, not sulforaphane itself. Conversion varies between people and preparations.

forms.name: Glucoraphanin with myrosinase
forms.note: Adds the converting enzyme. Enzyme activity and processing affect conversion; this is not automatically equivalent to preformed sulforaphane.

reference.noUpperLimit: No tolerable upper intake level for sulforaphane or broccoli extracts was found from EFSA or other official sources in the searches made for this guide. That is not proof that none exists, and not evidence that any amount is safe. Health Canada has licensing dose limits for some of these ingredients; they are product-licensing rules, not safety limits.

cautions: Sulforaphane preparations can cause nausea, heartburn or other digestive discomfort.
A burning sensation at the back of the throat has been reported with sulforaphane preparations.
Broccoli extract weight, glucoraphanin content and sulforaphane content are different label measurements. They cannot be treated as interchangeable amounts.
The source and formulation matter to safety as well as absorption; findings about one broccoli preparation cannot establish the safety of every concentrated supplement.

origin: Sulforaphane is formed when an enzyme, myrosinase, meets glucoraphanin, a compound in broccoli and other cruciferous vegetables. This happens when raw broccoli is chopped or chewed.
Broccoli sprouts and broccoli seed extract are rich in glucoraphanin. Cooking damages myrosinase, so how a food or supplement is prepared changes how much sulforaphane the body receives.
dosage: There is no reference intake and no upper limit for this ingredient. Studies measure different things (glucoraphanin, sulforaphane or the extract), so amounts are not interchangeable.
Amounts commonly used in studies and supplements are about 10 to 30 mg a day of sulforaphane from broccoli seed extract. This is not a reference intake or a personal recommendation.
Check whether the label states sulforaphane itself, glucoraphanin, or a broccoli extract weight, and whether the enzyme is included.

foodAmounts.verdict: Partly. Raw broccoli and broccoli sprouts are food sources, and studies show that chopping and the enzyme myrosinase largely decide how much sulforaphane you get. This guide has no checked figures for sulforaphane or glucoraphanin in foods, so it cannot say how much broccoli matches 10–30 mg.
foodAmounts.notChecked: The food table used by this app does not measure sulforaphane or glucoraphanin, so no per-food amounts are listed.
